title: Given an array containing `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `1` to `n` (or `0` to `n-1`), sort the array in place in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without using any sorting library. Explain the Cyclic Sort pattern and where it applies.
shortTitle: Cyclic Sort (Place Each Number at Its Correct Index)

s1_definition.profdef: Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range, typically `1..n` or `0..n-1`. Because every value has exactly one correct index (value `v` belongs at index `v-1`), the algorithm walks the array once and repeatedly swaps the current element to its rightful slot until the slot already holds the right value, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India numbers its night-deposit lockers 1 to n, and at closing a clerk finds the locker keys scattered on the counter. Key 5 belongs in locker 5, key 1 in locker 1. The clerk picks up whatever key is in front of them, walks it to its matching locker, and takes whatever key was already sitting there, repeating until the front slot holds the right key, then moves on. No key is carried twice unnecessarily, so the whole counter is tidied in one disciplined pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: When values are a permutation of `1..n`, the value itself tells you its home index, so one swap-until-correct pass sorts in linear time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range, typically `1..n` or `0..n-1`. Because every value has exactly one correct index (value `v` belongs at index `v-1`), the algorithm walks the array once and repeatedly swaps the current element to its rightful slot until the slot already holds the right value, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India numbers its night-deposit lockers 1 to n, and at closing a clerk finds the locker keys scattered on the counter. Key 5 belongs in locker 5, key 1 in locker 1. The clerk picks up whatever key is in front of them, walks it to its matching locker, and takes whatever key was already sitting there, repeating until the front slot holds the right key, then moves on. No key is carried twice unnecessarily, so the whole counter is tidied in one disciplined pass.

**One line to remember:** When values are a permutation of `1..n`, the value itself tells you its home index, so one swap-until-correct pass sorts in linear time.

sections.s2_technical:
The core invariant is that a number `v` in a `1..n` array must live at index `v-1`. The algorithm keeps a pointer `i` at the current position. It computes the target index `j = nums[i] - 1`. If `nums[i]` is not already sitting at its target (`nums[i] != nums[j]`), it swaps `nums[i]` with `nums[j]`. Crucially it does NOT advance `i` after a swap, because the element just moved into position `i` might itself be out of place. Only when `nums[i]` is already correct does it advance `i`.

The reason this is O(n) rather than O(n^2) despite the nested feel is amortized counting: each swap places at least one number into its final correct index permanently, and there are only `n` numbers, so at most `n` swaps happen across the entire run. For example, to settle account slots `int[] slots = {3,1,5,4,2};` the loop does `while (slots[i] != slots[slots[i]-1]) swap(slots, i, slots[i]-1);` and after the full pass `slots` becomes `{1,2,3,4,5}`.

A senior-level nuance is the guard condition. Comparing `nums[i] != nums[j]` rather than `i != j` makes the algorithm robust if duplicates ever appear, preventing an infinite swap loop between two equal values. For the strict `1..n` distinct case either guard works, but the value-comparison guard is the safer habit and is exactly what the duplicate-finding variants of this pattern rely on. The pattern only applies when the range is known and dense; it is not a general comparison sort.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the overnight batch produces a list of settlement sequence numbers that are supposed to be a clean 1 to n with no gaps, one per transaction in the day's batch. A feeder system delivers them shuffled, and before the reconciliation report can run, the operations team needs them arranged in order so each sequence number sits at its natural position for a fast index lookup. Re-running a full comparison sort every night on millions of numbers wastes CPU when the data is guaranteed to be a permutation of 1 to n. This is exactly how Cyclic Sort works: because each sequence number equals its own position plus one, we can place every number home in a single linear pass.

Problem 2 — The team also wants a reusable primitive, because the same place-it-at-its-index idea is about to power missing-number and duplicate detection in later batches. So we build a small `SettlementSequencer` with a `cyclicSort` method that other services can call.

The code will contain a `SettlementSequencer` class with a `cyclicSort(int[] seq)` method and a private `swap` helper, plus a `CyclicSortDemo` main that feeds a shuffled batch of Rajesh's and Priya's transaction sequence numbers and logs the sorted result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: `batch = {3,1,5,4,2}`.

Step 1: `i=0`, `seq[0]=3`, correct index is 2. `seq[2]=5` differs, so swap positions 0 and 2. Array becomes `{5,1,3,4,2}`. `i` stays at 0 because the new front value 5 may still be wrong.

Step 2: `i=0`, `seq[0]=5`, correct index is 4. `seq[4]=2` differs, swap positions 0 and 4. Array becomes `{2,1,3,4,5}`. `i` stays at 0.

Step 3: `i=0`, `seq[0]=2`, correct index is 1. `seq[1]=1` differs, swap 0 and 1. Array becomes `{1,2,3,4,5}`. `i` stays at 0.

Step 4: `i=0`, `seq[0]=1`, correct index is 0, and `seq[0]==seq[0]`, so advance `i` to 1. Positions 1 through 4 are each already correct, so `i` advances cleanly to the end.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Incoming settlement batch: [3, 1, 5, 4, 2]
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Sorted settlement batch:  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: batch = [3,1,5,4,2]  (permutation of 1..5)
    │
    ▼
  SettlementSequencer.cyclicSort()
    │ i=0: 3→idx2  swap        [5,1,3,4,2]
    │ i=0: 5→idx4  swap        [2,1,3,4,5]
    │ i=0: 2→idx1  swap        [1,2,3,4,5]
    │ i=0: 1 home → i++        (each later slot already home)
    ▼
  Output: [1,2,3,4,5]  — sorted in place, O(n) time, O(1) space
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cyclic Sort is an in-place linear-time technique that applies when the array values form a known dense range such as one to n. The defining insight is that each value has exactly one correct home index, namely the value minus one, so instead of comparing elements against each other I simply carry each value to its rightful slot. I keep a pointer at the current position, compute the target index from the value there, and swap it home if it is not already correct, and critically I do not advance the pointer after a swap because the element that just arrived may itself be misplaced.

The reason it runs in linear time rather than quadratic is amortized: every swap permanently settles at least one number into its final position, and there are only n numbers, so no more than n swaps ever occur across the whole run. I guard the swap with a value comparison rather than an index comparison, which keeps the loop safe even if duplicates sneak in, and that same place-it-at-its-index habit is what powers the missing-number and duplicate-detection variants of this pattern.

In my work at the National Bank of India I used this in the nightly settlement job. The batch delivered settlement sequence numbers that were guaranteed to be a permutation of one to n but arrived shuffled, and re-running a full comparison sort every night was wasteful. Cyclic Sort arranged them in a single disciplined pass with no extra memory, which kept the reconciliation window fast even on very large batches. What I stress to an interviewer is that recognizing the bounded-range precondition is the whole skill: the moment the values are a permutation of one to n, a general O(n log n) sort is the wrong tool and this pattern is the right one.
